subject: Website mistakes
label: CONTACT FORM DESIGN
caption_ig:
Stop treating your contact form like a job application. If you make people jump through hoops just to ask a question, they will hire your competitor instead. Delete the budget, timeline, and phone number fields today. Keep it simple: name, email, message. That's it.

#webdesign #conversionrate #smallbusinesstips #leadgeneration #userexperience
caption_fb: It's tempting to ask for every detail upfront on your contact form to filter out 'bad' leads. But this actually backfires. High-value clients are busy, and they value their privacy. When you force them to share their phone number or budget before they even know you, they just leave. Try reducing your form to name, email, and message. You can easily ask the qualifying questions during your first follow-up. Have you checked your own contact form lately?

slides.title: Your 7-field contact form is costing you sales.
slides.body: When busy prospects see a wall of text boxes, they don't fill them out. They close the tab and click the next business on Google.

slides.title: Asking for a budget upfront scares off buyers.
slides.body: High-value clients value privacy. Forcing them to share their budget or phone number before they even trust you makes them abandon the form entirely.

slides.title: Required phone number fields destroy your conversions.
slides.body: Most people hate getting unsolicited phone calls. Making the phone field mandatory forces prospects to choose between giving up their privacy or leaving your site.

slides.title: Delete every field except these three.
slides.body: Only ask for name, email, and their message. You can easily ask about budget, timelines, and phone numbers during your first email reply or discovery call.

slides.title: Treat your form like a handshake, not contracts.
slides.body: Your contact form's only job is to open a line of communication. Once you have their email, you can qualify them. Stop making them do homework first.
